title: Acute Respiratory Failure: Getting Oxygen In and Carbon Dioxide Out
summary: Why the same oxygen saturation can hide a failing lung, failing ventilation, or a failing respiratory pump, and how to use those differences to reason about support and its limits. Study material, not a protocol.
shareDescription: Why the same saturation can hide different failures of lung and respiratory pump, and how to reason about oxygen, high-flow and non-invasive support.

principles.title: Part I. The same saturation, three different failures
body: Three adults arrive in the same emergency department on the same evening. Like the patients in the Shock chapter, they are hypothetical, built for teaching, and revealed a little at a time. On the monitor they share one number: a peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) in the 80s, breathing room air. If that number were the whole story, each would get the same mask and the same plan.

Patient A is a woman in her fifties with three days of fever, cough, and pleuritic pain on the right. She is breathing fast, about 30 times a minute, and speaks in short phrases. There are bronchial breath sounds over the right lower chest. Patient B is a man in his thirties found drowsy at home beside an empty pill bottle. His pupils are small, his breathing is slow and shallow, and his chest sounds clear. Patient C is a man in his late sixties with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) who has been more breathless for four days. He sits forward with his hands on his knees, his neck muscles tighten with each breath, he breathes out through pursed lips, and the expiration seems never to finish before the next breath begins.

The shared saturation tells us that the hemoglobin passing the probe carries less oxygen than usual. It does not tell us why. In A, blood is crossing lung that has filled with inflammatory fluid and receives no fresh gas. In B, the lungs are probably normal, but too little air is moving through them. In C, a lung with narrowed airways and lost elastic recoil is placing a load on breathing muscles that may be near the limit of what they can sustain. Three different mechanisms, three different responses to oxygen, and three different dangers that oxygen alone could hide.

This chapter follows them through the physiology needed to tell those mechanisms apart: how carbon dioxide leaves the body, the five ways arterial blood ends up short of oxygen, the mechanics and endurance of the respiratory pump, what bedside measurements can and cannot show, and how support should be matched to the failing part. It explains principles of support. It is not a ventilator handbook or an airway manual.

principles.title: What respiratory failure is, and why the thresholds are conventions
body: Respiratory failure is a failure of gas exchange to meet the body's needs: oxygen is not reaching arterial blood in sufficient quantity, carbon dioxide is not being removed fast enough, or both. Like shock, it is defined by function rather than by a single number. The blood gas is how we document it, but the failure lives in the lung, in the pump that ventilates the lung, or in the relationship between the two and the body's demand.

By convention, hypoxemic respiratory failure is often described as an arterial oxygen tension (PaO2) below about 60 mm Hg breathing room air, and hypercapnic respiratory failure as an arterial carbon dioxide tension (PaCO2) above about 45 to 50 mm Hg with acidemia. These cut-offs are useful for communication and for trials. They are not diagnoses. A PaO2 of 62 mm Hg in someone whose respiratory rate is climbing and who is tiring is more worrying than a PaO2 of 58 mm Hg in someone stable on chronic home oxygen, and a PaCO2 of 60 mm Hg means something quite different with a normal pH than with a pH of 7.20.

Two broad types are usually named. Type 1, hypoxemic failure, is a problem of getting oxygen across a diseased lung; PaCO2 is normal or low, because the same patient often breathes harder and blows off carbon dioxide. Type 2, hypercapnic failure, is a problem of moving enough gas in and out; PaCO2 rises, and hypoxemia follows, partly as arithmetic. Many patients have both, and many have an acute illness laid over chronic disease, so the label is a starting point for reasoning rather than a category to file the patient in.

It helps to treat the respiratory system as two organs. The lung is the gas-exchanging surface, where ventilation and blood flow must meet. The pump is everything that moves gas to and from that surface: the brainstem that generates drive, the nerves and neuromuscular junctions that carry it, the diaphragm and other muscles that contract, and the chest wall and abdomen they act against. A failing lung usually shows itself first as hypoxemia. A failing pump shows itself as hypoventilation and, with it, rising carbon dioxide. Patient A has a lung problem, Patient B a pump problem at its very top, in the drive, and Patient C a combination in which a sick lung is overloading a pump that is starting to fail.
To tell these apart we start with the more forgiving gas, carbon dioxide, because its behavior is governed by a single quantity.

principles.title: Part II. Getting carbon dioxide out
body: Carbon dioxide is produced continuously by metabolism and carried to the lungs in venous blood. Its arterial tension is set by a balance between how fast it is made and how fast fresh gas washes it out of the alveoli. That makes PaCO2 the most direct readout we have of whether ventilation is adequate for the body's needs. It is not a readout of how hard the patient is breathing, and the difference between the two is the subject of this part.

principles.title: Alveolar ventilation: the breath that counts
body: Only part of each breath reaches gas-exchanging alveoli. The rest fills the conducting airways, the trachea and bronchi, and leaves again unchanged. That wasted volume is the anatomic dead space, about 150 mL in an average adult, and it is roughly fixed for a given person regardless of how large each breath is. Some gas that does reach alveoli is also wasted, because it arrives at units with little or no blood flow. Anatomic and this alveolar dead space together make up the physiological dead space, usually expressed as a fraction of the tidal volume, VD/VT.

Minute ventilation (VE), the respiratory rate multiplied by the tidal volume, is what a spirometer or ventilator reports. Alveolar ventilation (VA) is the part that does useful work: VA = VE × (1 − VD/VT). At steady state, PaCO2 is proportional to carbon dioxide production divided by alveolar ventilation: PaCO2 = 0.863 × VCO2 / VA, with VCO2 in mL/min at standard conditions, VA in L/min at body conditions, and 0.863 the constant that reconciles those units. The equation says something simple. If production is unchanged, halving alveolar ventilation doubles PaCO2, and doubling it halves PaCO2. Nothing in the equation mentions effort.

This is why a patient can breathe very fast and still retain carbon dioxide. Rapid shallow breathing spends a larger share of each breath on the fixed anatomic dead space, and lung disease can raise the alveolar part of the dead space as well. Respiratory rate alone therefore says nothing about effective ventilation: it has to be read together with the size of each breath and the share of each breath that is wasted. Two patients can move the same six liters a minute and achieve very different alveolar ventilation, as the worked example shows. The trap at the bedside is to look at a high respiratory rate, see a lot of work, and assume a lot of ventilation.

The equation describes a steady state. When ventilation changes abruptly, PaCO2 moves toward its new level over minutes, not instantly, because the body holds a large store of carbon dioxide, much of it as bicarbonate, that must fill or empty. A patient who has just become apneic does not reach a high PaCO2 within seconds, and a patient who has just been ventilated more vigorously does not normalize at once. Blood-gas values drawn shortly after a change sit somewhere along that path.

questions.prompt: A patient's minute ventilation is unchanged at 10 L/min over two hours, yet PaCO2 has risen from 40 to 55 mm Hg. What could have changed?
questions.answer: Either carbon dioxide production has risen, or alveolar ventilation has fallen while minute ventilation stayed the same, or both. Alveolar ventilation can fall at constant minute ventilation if breaths become smaller and faster, so more of each breath is spent on anatomic dead space, or if alveolar dead space rises, as with a pulmonary embolus, a fall in cardiac output, or overdistension of ventilated units. Production rises with fever, shivering, agitation, or high-carbohydrate feeding. Separating these needs the tidal volume pattern, a sense of metabolic state, and, where available, the gap between end-tidal and arterial carbon dioxide, which widens as alveolar dead space rises.
questions.causalChain: PaCO2 is proportional to VCO2 divided by VA; VA = VE × (1 − VD/VT); a constant VE with a rising VD/VT or a rising VCO2 raises PaCO2.
questions.assumption: That both values reflect a steady state and that the two samples were measured comparably.
questions.misconception: That minute ventilation measures how well carbon dioxide is being cleared. It measures gas moved, not gas exchanged.

workedExample.title: Worked example: the same minute ventilation, different alveolar ventilation
body: These numbers are illustrative, chosen to make the arithmetic visible, and assume a steady state with carbon dioxide production held constant.

**Slow, deep breathing.** Respiratory rate 12/min, tidal volume 500 mL, minute ventilation 6.0 L/min. With an anatomic dead space of 150 mL, each breath delivers 350 mL to alveoli, so VA = 12 × 0.35 = 4.2 L/min. If PaCO2 is 40 mm Hg here, VCO2 = 40 × 4.2 / 0.863 ≈ 195 mL/min, an ordinary resting value.

**Fast, shallow breathing.** Respiratory rate 30/min, tidal volume 200 mL, minute ventilation again 6.0 L/min. With the same 150 mL dead space, each breath delivers 50 mL, so VA = 30 × 0.05 = 1.5 L/min.

**Consequence.** Alveolar ventilation has fallen from 4.2 to 1.5 L/min, a factor of about 2.8. At the same VCO2, steady-state PaCO2 would rise by the same factor, from 40 toward about 110 mm Hg. The real patient would not reach that steady state calmly, and dead space is not perfectly fixed at very small tidal volumes, but the direction and the scale are the point: the same minute ventilation can hide a large loss of effective ventilation.

**A second route to the same result.** Hold minute ventilation at 10 L/min. With VD/VT 0.3, VA = 10 × 0.7 = 7 L/min. If dead-space fraction rises to 0.6, from more wasted ventilation rather than smaller breaths, VA = 10 × 0.4 = 4 L/min. At constant VCO2 (here about 325 mL/min, as in a febrile patient), PaCO2 rises from 40 to 40 × 7/4 = 70 mm Hg, with no change in rate, tidal volume, or effort.

principles.title: Dead space: ventilation that reaches no blood
body: Alveolar dead space is the high end of the ventilation-perfusion spectrum: units receive gas but little or no blood, so the gas leaves as it arrived and carries no carbon dioxide away. A pulmonary embolus is the textbook example, but the commonest causes in a resuscitation room are quieter. When cardiac output falls, perfusion of the upper, less dependent lung falls with it, and more ventilated units become underperfused. When positive pressure overdistends some alveoli, their capillaries are compressed and their blood is diverted elsewhere. The heart-lung interactions described in the Shock chapter, Part VII, run in both directions: the circulation changes how much of ventilation is useful, just as ventilation changes the circulation.

Dead space is one reason why a rising PaCO2 in a critically ill patient should prompt a look at the circulation as well as the lungs. It is also why end-tidal carbon dioxide, measured at the mouth, can fall below arterial PaCO2 by a widening margin: gas from unperfused units dilutes the gas exhaled from perfused ones.

What PaCO2 alone cannot tell us is the cause of its rise. A high value is compatible with reduced drive, a weak or overloaded pump, increased dead space, increased production, or a combination. Patient B and Patient C may both arrive with a high PaCO2, and the reasons have almost nothing in common. That is the first thing the number withholds.

questions.prompt: A ventilated patient bleeds rapidly and his cardiac output falls, with no change in ventilator settings. What would you expect to happen to end-tidal carbon dioxide and to the gap between it and arterial PaCO2?
questions.answer: End-tidal carbon dioxide should fall, often quickly, and the arterial to end-tidal gap should widen. Less blood reaches the lungs, so less carbon dioxide is delivered to the alveoli each minute, and the less dependent units become ventilated but underperfused, which is alveolar dead space. Gas from those units dilutes exhaled gas. Arterial PaCO2 may stay similar or rise, because tissue carbon dioxide is still being produced and less of it is being cleared. A falling end-tidal value here is a sign of the circulation, not of better ventilation.
questions.causalChain: Falling cardiac output reduces pulmonary blood flow; carbon dioxide delivery to the lungs falls; perfusion of upper units falls; alveolar dead space rises; exhaled gas is diluted; end-tidal falls more than arterial PaCO2.
questions.assumption: That minute ventilation, metabolic rate, and the sampling line are unchanged.
questions.misconception: That a falling end-tidal value always means the patient is being over-ventilated.

principles.title: Part III. Getting oxygen in: the five mechanisms of hypoxemia
body: Oxygen has a harder journey than carbon dioxide, and it helps to name each stage. The inspired partial pressure (PIO2) is set by the gas we breathe and the barometric pressure. The alveolar partial pressure (PAO2) is what remains after that gas is humidified and mixed with the carbon dioxide arriving from the blood. The arterial partial pressure (PaO2) is the tension of oxygen dissolved in blood leaving the lung. Saturation (SaO2) is the fraction of hemoglobin carrying oxygen, and oxygen content (CaO2) is the total amount carried per deciliter, almost all of it on hemoglobin: about 1.34 × hemoglobin × SaO2, plus a small dissolved part of 0.003 × PaO2. Hypoxemia can arise at five points: too little oxygen inspired, too little ventilation of the alveoli, ventilation and blood flow poorly matched, blood bypassing ventilated alveoli altogether, and oxygen failing to cross the alveolar wall in time. These mechanisms respond differently to supplemental oxygen and leave different fingerprints in the relation between alveolar and arterial oxygen. That relation begins with an estimate of what the alveolus contains.

principles.title: The alveolar gas equation and the A–a gradient
body: Inspired gas is warmed and saturated with water vapor on its way down, so the partial pressure of oxygen entering the alveoli is the inspired fraction (FiO2) multiplied by barometric pressure (PB) less water vapor pressure (PH2O): FiO2 × (PB − PH2O). In the alveolus, oxygen is continuously removed and carbon dioxide added. The simplified alveolar gas equation accounts for this: PAO2 = FiO2 × (PB − PH2O) − PaCO2/R, where R, the respiratory quotient, is the ratio of carbon dioxide produced to oxygen consumed. The usual working assumptions are PB 760 mm Hg at sea level, PH2O 47 mm Hg at body temperature, and R 0.8. At altitude PB is lower, and the whole calculation shifts.

The equation carries one of the most important ideas in this chapter. Alveolar carbon dioxide displaces alveolar oxygen. If ventilation falls and PaCO2 rises, PAO2 must fall even when the lung itself is perfectly healthy. Hypoxemia can therefore be pure arithmetic.

The difference between the calculated alveolar PAO2 and the measured arterial PaO2 is the alveolar-arterial (A–a) gradient. In healthy young adults breathing room air it is small, usually under about 10 to 15 mm Hg, and it rises with age. One common rule of thumb puts the upper limit of normal at about age/4 + 4 mm Hg, roughly 21 mm Hg at 68, but this is an approximate population range and not a value to subtract from an individual patient's result as if it were measured. A clearly widened gradient in a hypoxemic patient says that the lung is failing to pass on what the alveolus holds. A normal gradient says that the hypoxemia can be explained without a gas-transfer defect, so the problem probably lies upstream, in how much oxygen reaches the alveolus. It does not say the lungs are healthy: in a study of patients with suspected pulmonary embolism, a gradient inside the normal range did not exclude the diagnosis.

The gradient has real limits. The calculated PAO2 is an idealized average for a lung imagined as one uniform unit; a diseased lung contains units with very different alveolar oxygen, and no single number describes them all. Because the calculation rests on assumed values for R and PB, small gradients should not be read too precisely. The gradient also widens with FiO2 even when the lung has not changed, because the same degree of mismatch produces a larger absolute difference when alveolar oxygen is high, so a gradient measured on supplemental oxygen cannot be compared with a room-air reference. The ratio of PaO2 to FiO2, widely used as a severity measure, has related problems: it varies with FiO2 and with positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) for the same lung, so it describes a patient on a particular level of support rather than the lung in isolation.

questions.prompt: Patient B is given oxygen by face mask and his SpO2 rises from about 80 to 98 percent within minutes. What is still unknown?
questions.answer: Whether he is ventilating any better. His hypoxemia came from a high alveolar carbon dioxide displacing oxygen, with a normal A–a gradient. Raising FiO2 increases alveolar oxygen directly and corrects the saturation easily, but it does nothing to his alveolar ventilation. His PaCO2 may be the same or still rising, and his pH falling, while the oximeter looks reassuring. The cause of the hypoventilation, the drug, is also still acting. The saturation now tells us almost nothing about the problem that will harm him.
questions.causalChain: Opioid reduces central drive; alveolar ventilation falls; PaCO2 rises; PAO2 falls by PaCO2/R; supplemental oxygen raises FiO2 × (PB − PH2O) and restores PAO2 and SpO2; alveolar ventilation and PaCO2 are unaffected.
questions.assumption: That his lungs are otherwise normal, as his clear chest and normal gradient suggest, and that no aspiration has occurred.
questions.misconception: That a normal saturation on oxygen means adequate breathing.
questions.missingData: Respiratory rate and depth, mental status, a blood gas or capnography for carbon dioxide, and whether reversible drug effect has been treated.

questions.prompt: A resident looks at Patient C's room-air gas (PaCO2 62, PaO2 56 mm Hg, A–a gradient about 16 mm Hg) and says: "The gradient proves V/Q mismatch on top of his hypoventilation." Is that conclusion supported?
questions.answer: No. At 68, a gradient of about 16 mm Hg falls within the rough age-expected range, and it is under 20 mm Hg even without adjustment. The calculation also rests on assumed values for R and barometric pressure, so a difference of a few mm Hg carries little weight. What the gas shows strongly is hypoventilation: his raised PaCO2 accounts for nearly all of the fall in alveolar and arterial oxygen. He very likely does have mismatched units, given his COPD, his air trapping, and his work of breathing, but that belief rests on the history and examination, not on this gradient. The opposite error is also possible: a normal gradient does not show that his lungs are healthy.
questions.causalChain: PaCO2 62 lowers PAO2 to about 72 mm Hg; PaO2 56 leaves a gradient of about 16 mm Hg; the age-expected upper limit is roughly 21 mm Hg; the gas is explained by hypoventilation without needing a transfer defect; the gradient neither proves nor excludes mismatch.
questions.assumption: That the sample is arterial, on room air, at sea level, and that R is close to 0.8.
questions.misconception: That a single A–a value establishes the mechanism, in either direction.

workedExample.title: Worked example: the three patients' gradients
body: All values assume sea level (PB 760 mm Hg), PH2O 47 mm Hg, and R 0.8, so FiO2 × (PB − PH2O) on room air is 0.21 × 713 ≈ 150 mm Hg. The patients' values are illustrative.
**A healthy reference.** Room air, PaCO2 40 mm Hg: PAO2 = 150 − 40/0.8 = 150 − 50 = 100 mm Hg. A PaO2 of 90 mm Hg gives an A–a gradient of about 10 mm Hg.

**Patient B, opioid hypoventilation, on room air.** PaCO2 70 mm Hg: PAO2 = 0.21 × (760 − 47) − 70/0.8 = 149.7 − 87.5 ≈ 62 mm Hg. His measured PaO2 is about 56 mm Hg, so the A–a gradient is about 6 mm Hg, which is normal. All of his hypoxemia is explained by the carbon dioxide occupying his alveoli. A PaO2 of 56 mm Hg corresponds to a saturation of about 88 percent on a standard curve at pH 7.40. At his pH of about 7.21, the rightward shift brings the predicted value to roughly 80 percent (see Part V).

**Patient A, pneumonia, on room air.** PaCO2 32 mm Hg, because she is breathing fast: PAO2 = 150 − 32/0.8 = 150 − 40 = 110 mm Hg. Her PaO2 is 55 mm Hg, so the gradient is about 55 mm Hg. Her alveolar oxygen is higher than normal, and her blood still leaves the lung poorly oxygenated: the lung is failing to transfer it.

**Patient A after a change to FiO2 1.0.** At FiO2 1.0, and assuming her PaCO2 stays at 32 mm Hg, PAO2 is about 713 − 32/0.8 ≈ 673 mm Hg. If her PaO2 rises only to about 70 mm Hg, the gradient is now about 600 mm Hg. The large number reflects both the high FiO2 and the shunt, and it cannot be compared with her room-air value. The useful observation is the small change in PaO2 for a large change in inspired oxygen.

**Patient C, COPD exacerbation, on room air.** PaCO2 62 mm Hg: PAO2 = 149.7 − 62/0.8 = 149.7 − 77.5 ≈ 72 mm Hg. His PaO2 is 56 mm Hg, so the gradient is about 16 mm Hg. For a man of 68 that sits inside the rough age-expected range of about 21 mm Hg, and it is under 20 mm Hg even before any age adjustment. His gas is explained almost entirely by hypoventilation. His history and his mechanics make abnormal ventilation-perfusion matching very likely, but this gradient does not by itself prove it.

principles.title: Ventilation-perfusion mismatch and shunt
body: In a healthy lung, ventilation and blood flow are not perfectly matched, but they are close: the ratio of ventilation to perfusion (V/Q) clusters around one across most units. In disease the distribution spreads. Units with high V/Q waste ventilation and behave as dead space. Units with low V/Q receive some fresh gas, but not enough for the blood flowing past them, so that blood leaves only partly oxygenated. At the extreme are units with no ventilation at all, through which blood passes unchanged. That extreme is shunt. Shunt is the zero-ventilation end of the same spectrum, and it is counted as a separate mechanism because it responds to oxygen so differently.

That difference is the reason Patient A matters. In a low V/Q unit, adding oxygen raises the alveolar oxygen tension even though the gas arrives slowly, and the blood passing that unit eventually becomes well saturated. Low V/Q hypoxemia therefore usually responds to modest supplemental oxygen. In a shunting unit, filled with pus or fluid or collapsed, no inspired gas arrives. Blood passing it never meets the added oxygen. When it rejoins blood from healthy units, what mixes is oxygen content, not partial pressure, and the healthy units cannot make up the shortfall: their hemoglobin is already nearly saturated on room air, and extra oxygen in solution adds very little.

A rough calculation shows the size of the effect. Assume a hemoglobin of 15 g/dL, a mixed venous saturation of 70 percent, and that 30 percent of pulmonary blood flow passes through unventilated lung while the rest meets healthy units. Blood from the shunt carries about 14 mL of oxygen per deciliter. On room air, blood from the healthy units carries about 20 mL/dL. The mixture carries about 18 mL/dL, which corresponds to a PaO2 near 58 mm Hg. On 100 percent oxygen the healthy units' PO2 rises to about 660 mm Hg, but their content rises only to about 22 mL/dL. The mixture reaches about 19.7 mL/dL, a PaO2 in the high 80s if mixed venous content stays fixed, and higher, though still under 150 mm Hg, at a normal steady state where venous content rises. Both are far below the more than 400 mm Hg that averaging the partial pressures would predict. Oxygen helped, but far less than the alveolar numbers suggest, and the response shrinks as the shunt fraction grows. These numbers depend on the stated assumptions and are illustrative.

The lung defends itself against low V/Q in part through hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction: small pulmonary arteries supplying poorly ventilated regions constrict in response to low alveolar oxygen, diverting blood toward better-ventilated lung. The response is real but partial, and its strength varies between people and conditions. Anything that relaxes it can worsen matching. High inspired oxygen can raise alveolar oxygen in poorly ventilated units enough to release the constriction, and systemic vasodilators can blunt it. In patients whose gas exchange depends on that diversion, such as Patient C, this is one way oxygen can worsen carbon dioxide retention, a subject we return to in Part VI.

One further amplifier links this chapter to the Shock chapter, Part V. Shunted blood leaves the lung with the oxygen content it arrived with, the mixed venous content. If cardiac output falls or oxygen consumption rises, tissues extract more, mixed venous content falls, and the shunted blood is even less oxygenated when it rejoins the arterial stream. The same shunt fraction can then produce a lower PaO2. A falling PaO2 in a patient with a fixed shunt is not necessarily a worsening lung; it can be a failing circulation. How large the effect is depends on the shunt fraction, being greatest when the shunt is large.

Real patients rarely have pure shunt or pure mismatch. Pneumonia, atelectasis, and edema usually produce both, so the response to oxygen is graded rather than all or nothing. It depends on the shunt fraction, the FiO2 actually delivered, whether collapsed lung can be recruited, the mixed venous oxygen content, and a circulation that may be changing at the same time. A poor response points toward shunt, and a brisk one argues against a large shunt, but the response informs the reasoning about mechanism. It is not a diagnostic test on its own.

questions.prompt: Patient A's FiO2 is increased from 0.4 to 1.0, and her PaO2 rises only from 62 to 70 mm Hg. What does that suggest?
questions.answer: That a large part of her hypoxemia probably comes from shunt rather than from low V/Q. If poorly ventilated but still ventilated units were the main problem, raising FiO2 would raise their alveolar oxygen and her PaO2 would rise substantially. Blood crossing consolidated lung never meets the added oxygen, and the well-ventilated units were already near full saturation, so more oxygen changes arterial content little. This is an inference, not a measurement: a falling mixed venous content or a delivered FiO2 lower than the set value could produce the same small response. If those are reasonable, the next useful moves are those that address the shunt itself, such as recruiting or clearing affected lung where that is possible, rather than ever-higher FiO2.
questions.causalChain: Consolidation leaves units perfused but unventilated; blood crossing them is not exposed to inspired oxygen; added FiO2 raises PAO2 only in ventilated units, which were already near saturation; arterial content and PaO2 change little.
questions.assumption: That her mixed venous oxygen content and cardiac output did not change meaningfully between the two measurements, and that the FiO2 delivered was close to the FiO2 set.
questions.misconception: That a poor response to oxygen means not enough oxygen is being given, or that it proves shunt by itself. It suggests the oxygen is not reaching the blood that needs it.

principles.title: Diffusion limitation and low inspired oxygen
body: Two further mechanisms complete the list. Diffusion limitation occurs when oxygen cannot equilibrate across the alveolar-capillary barrier during the time a red cell spends in the capillary. At rest the healthy reserve is usually large enough that equilibration is still reached, so diffusion limitation is rarely the dominant cause of resting hypoxemia. It becomes important during exercise, when transit time shortens, at altitude, when the driving pressure is low, and in some interstitial diseases. It widens the A–a gradient and generally corrects with oxygen.

Low inspired oxygen is the simplest mechanism of all: at altitude, or in an enclosed space where oxygen has been consumed or displaced, the inspired partial pressure is low. The A–a gradient is normal, PaCO2 is often low as breathing increases, and oxygen corrects it.

Hypoventilation, which we met in Patient B, and the two ends of the V/Q spectrum, low V/Q mismatch and shunt, make up the other three. Hypoventilation is the only mechanism in which the main abnormality is in PaCO2, and the gradient stays normal unless lung disease is also present. The table brings the five together. Real patients mix them, so the table describes dominant patterns rather than exclusive categories.

questions.prompt: A hiker is hypoxemic on arrival at a mountain clinic with a normal A–a gradient calculated at that clinic's barometric pressure and a low PaCO2. Which mechanisms are most and least likely?
questions.answer: Low inspired oxygen is most likely, perhaps with a contribution from diffusion limitation on exertion. Hypoventilation is unlikely, because PaCO2 is low rather than high. A normal gradient argues against substantial shunt or low V/Q mismatch at this point. Had the calculation been done with a sea-level PB of 760 mm Hg, PAO2 would have been overestimated and the gradient would have looked falsely wide.
questions.causalChain: Lower PB lowers inspired and alveolar oxygen; hypoxemia stimulates ventilation and lowers PaCO2; a healthy lung transfers the reduced alveolar oxygen normally, so the gradient stays normal.
questions.assumption: That PB was measured or estimated correctly for the altitude and that the patient has no hidden lung disease such as early high-altitude pulmonary edema.
questions.misconception: That a normal gradient means there is no problem. It means the problem is not in the gas-exchanging lung.

principles.title: Part IV. The pump: mechanics, work of breathing, and fatigue
body: Some patients fail not because the lung cannot exchange gas but because the muscles can no longer keep up with what is being asked of them. Understanding this kind of failure means understanding the load the pump faces, its capacity to meet it, and how both change during an illness. This is where Patient C's danger lies.

principles.title: Compliance, resistance, and the pressure to breathe
body: Each breath requires the respiratory muscles, or a ventilator, to generate pressure. That pressure has to do two things. It must stretch the lung and chest wall against their elastic recoil, and it must drive gas through the airways against their resistance. Compliance describes the first: the change in volume for each unit change in distending pressure. A stiff lung, filled with fluid or scar, has low compliance and needs more pressure for the same tidal volume. Resistance describes the second: the pressure needed per unit of flow. Narrowed, inflamed, or secretion-filled airways raise resistance, and faster flows need disproportionately more pressure.

Put in words, the equation of motion of the respiratory system says that the pressure needed for a breath is the sum of an elastic part, proportional to volume and inversely to compliance, and a resistive part, proportional to flow and resistance, plus any pressure needed to overcome positive pressure already trapped in the alveoli at the end of expiration. Patients with stiff lungs tend to choose small, rapid breaths, which keep the elastic load per breath low. Patients with high resistance tend to choose slower, longer breaths, which reduce flow. Both choices make sense, and both have costs: rapid shallow breathing wastes ventilation on dead space, and slow breathing may not be possible if expiration cannot be completed.

In a patient on a ventilator these quantities can be estimated during a brief pause at the end of inspiration, when flow is zero and the resistive component disappears. The worked example shows the arithmetic. In a spontaneously breathing patient they cannot be measured this way, and we infer them from the pattern of breathing, the sounds, and the effort.

workedExample.title: Worked example: reading compliance and resistance on a ventilator
body: Illustrative values in a patient on volume-controlled ventilation with constant inspiratory flow and no spontaneous effort.

**Settings and readings.** Tidal volume 450 mL; set PEEP 10 cm H2O; inspiratory flow 60 L/min, which is 1 L/s; peak airway pressure 40 cm H2O; plateau pressure, during an end-inspiratory pause, 30 cm H2O.

**Static compliance.** Volume divided by the elastic pressure change: 450 / (30 − 10) = 22.5 mL/cm H2O. This assumes no intrinsic PEEP; if gas is trapped, the true end-expiratory pressure is higher than the set PEEP and compliance is underestimated by this calculation.
**Airway resistance.** The pressure that disappears when flow stops, divided by flow: (40 − 30) / 1 = 10 cm H2O/L/s.

**Interpretation.** A low compliance points toward stiff lung or chest wall; a high resistance points toward the airways or the tube. These are estimates for one set of conditions. They describe the whole respiratory system, lung and chest wall together, and do not by themselves say which is responsible.

principles.title: Air trapping, intrinsic PEEP, and the asthma contrast
body: Patient C's narrowed airways and lost elastic recoil mean that, during expiration, flow is limited: beyond a certain point, pushing harder does not empty the lung faster, because the airways collapse further. If the next breath begins before expiration is complete, some gas stays behind. Over successive breaths the end-expiratory lung volume climbs until a new balance is reached at a higher volume. This is dynamic hyperinflation. The alveolar pressure at the end of expiration is now above atmospheric pressure. That trapped pressure is intrinsic PEEP, sometimes called auto-PEEP.

Intrinsic PEEP imposes a threshold load. Air flows in only when alveolar pressure falls below the pressure at the airway opening, so each inspiratory effort must first lower alveolar pressure by the amount of the trapped pressure before any gas moves. Each breath begins with work that moves no gas. Hyperinflation also places the diaphragm at a mechanical disadvantage: flattened and shortened, it generates less pressure for the same activation. A faster respiratory rate, driven by distress or hypoxemia, shortens expiratory time, and because expiratory flow is already limited, the trapping worsens. The loop is self-reinforcing, and it is the reason a patient like C can deteriorate quickly once it starts.

Raised intrathoracic pressure has circulatory consequences too. As the Shock chapter describes in Part VII, a rise in pleural pressure impedes venous return. In severe air trapping, especially once positive-pressure ventilation is started, hypotension can follow, and allowing longer expiratory time can restore it. That interaction belongs to both chapters.

Acute severe asthma shares this mechanism: air trapping, intrinsic PEEP, threshold loading, and the same circulatory risk. It differs in what the carbon dioxide usually shows. Early in an asthma attack, the patient typically hyperventilates and PaCO2 is low. A PaCO2 that is normal, or rising, in someone who is still working hard to breathe is therefore not reassuring. It suggests that ventilation is failing to keep up with demand, through tiring, worsening obstruction, or both, and it calls for closer attention rather than relief. In COPD, by contrast, a raised PaCO2 may be chronic, and the pH and the trend carry more information than the absolute value.

questions.prompt: A young woman with acute asthma has a respiratory rate of 28/min and is using her neck muscles. Her PaCO2 is 41 mm Hg. Why is this value worrying?
questions.answer: Because in a patient breathing this hard, with obstruction, the expected PaCO2 early in an attack is low, from hyperventilation. A value in the normal range means alveolar ventilation is no longer exceeding the needs of carbon dioxide clearance despite high effort. That can reflect worsening obstruction, tiring muscles, rising dead space from hyperinflation, or a combination. It points toward impending ventilatory failure, and it calls for closer observation and escalation of treatment rather than reassurance.
questions.causalChain: Obstruction and air trapping raise the work of breathing; early on, drive and effort raise alveolar ventilation and lower PaCO2; as load outpaces capacity or dead space rises, alveolar ventilation falls back toward and below demand; PaCO2 normalizes and then rises.
questions.assumption: That this is acute asthma without chronic carbon dioxide retention and that the sample is arterial and current.
questions.misconception: That a normal number means a normal state. In context, a normal PaCO2 is an abnormal finding.

questions.prompt: As Patient C becomes more distressed, his respiratory rate rises from 24 to 34/min. Predict the effect on his air trapping and on the work of each breath.
questions.answer: Air trapping should worsen. A faster rate shortens the time available for expiration, and because his expiratory flow is limited, less of each breath is exhaled before the next begins. End-expiratory volume and intrinsic PEEP rise, so each breath starts with a larger threshold load, and the diaphragm is flattened further and works at a greater mechanical disadvantage. Tidal volume is likely to fall, raising the dead-space fraction. More effort buys less alveolar ventilation, which is the self-reinforcing loop described above.
questions.causalChain: Higher rate shortens expiratory time; flow-limited expiration is incomplete; end-expiratory volume and intrinsic PEEP rise; threshold load and diaphragmatic disadvantage increase; tidal volume falls and VD/VT rises; alveolar ventilation falls despite more effort.
questions.assumption: That his airway obstruction has not changed in the same period and that inspiratory time does not shorten enough to offset the change.
questions.misconception: That breathing faster always means ventilating more.

principles.title: Load, capacity, and fatigue
body: The pump fails when the load placed on it persistently exceeds its capacity to meet that load. Load rises with stiffer lungs, narrower airways, intrinsic PEEP, increased ventilatory demand from fever, acidosis, or sepsis, and increased dead space that forces more ventilation for the same carbon dioxide clearance. Capacity falls with hyperinflation, which weakens the diaphragm mechanically, with electrolyte disturbance, malnutrition, shock that limits blood flow to the muscles, and neuromuscular disease. Drive, the third element, can be too low, as in Patient B, or very high, as in a frightened, hypoxemic patient whose muscles are working near their maximum.

Respiratory muscles, like other skeletal muscles, can fatigue when the work they sustain is high relative to their maximum for long enough. How quickly this happens, and how much of what clinicians call fatigue is true contractile fatigue rather than a protective reduction in central drive, are debated questions, reviewed by Laghi and Tobin. What is clearer is the clinical pattern: a patient who has been working hard for hours may show a rising respiratory rate, recruitment of accessory muscles, abdominal paradox in which the abdomen moves inward on inspiration, inability to speak in sentences, and changes in mental state. A rising PaCO2 often comes late in this sequence, after these signs have been present for some time. Waiting for it can mean waiting too long.

Rapid shallow breathing is both a sign and a mechanism here. It is how an overloaded pump reduces the work of each breath, and it raises the dead-space fraction, so the patient needs still more minute ventilation to clear the same carbon dioxide.

One further idea is contested, and it is presented here as a hypothesis rather than an established mechanism. In hypoxemic patients breathing spontaneously with very high effort, large swings in pleural pressure may stretch an already injured lung and add to the injury, a process sometimes called patient self-inflicted lung injury. The physiological reasoning is plausible, and it is part of the argument for not leaving a patient struggling indefinitely, but how often it occurs and how much it matters clinically is not settled.

diagram.caption: The respiratory pump: load against capacity
diagram.alt: One causal loop, read clockwise, under the statement that the pump fails when load persistently exceeds its capacity to meet that load. Load rises, so effort increases; sustained high effort fatigues the muscles; capacity falls; PaCO2 rises; and an arrow labeled acidosis raises ventilatory demand returns to rising load. Load and effort are drawn as solid red boxes, fatigue and falling capacity as dashed teal boxes, and rising PaCO2 as a gold box. Notes accompanying the loop: load rises with stiffer lungs, narrower airways, intrinsic PEEP, ventilatory demand from fever, acidosis or sepsis, and dead space forcing more ventilation. Rapid shallow breathing reduces the work of each breath but raises the dead-space fraction. A rising PaCO2 often comes late; waiting for it can mean waiting too long. Conceptual loop; no scale.

principles.title: Vignette: pump failure with clear lungs
body: A woman in her forties presents with four days of ascending weakness in the legs, now affecting her arms, and a soft voice. Her oxygen saturation is normal on room air, her chest is clear, and her blood gas is unremarkable. A rapidly progressive neuropathy such as Guillain-Barré syndrome is suspected.

Her lungs are normal, and that is the trap. The gas exchange looks reassuring because the failing part is the pump, and pump weakness may show nothing in SpO2 or PaCO2 until it is advanced. The useful measurements are of the pump's strength: forced vital capacity and maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures measured at the bedside, followed as a trend over hours, together with her ability to cough, swallow, and protect her airway. A falling vital capacity is a warning that comes earlier than any blood gas, and the direction and speed of the fall matter more than any single value.

principles.title: Part V. What bedside measurements can and cannot tell you
body: Each of the three patients will be followed with the same instruments: an oximeter, perhaps a capnograph, blood gases, and the clinician's eyes. Each instrument measures something specific, with its own confounders and its own timescale. Reading them well means knowing what each one leaves out, and which question each one answers. SpO2 asks whether arterial hemoglobin is adequately saturated under the oxygen support being given. PaCO2 and pH ask whether ventilation is keeping up with carbon dioxide production, and what that does to acid–base balance. The pattern and effort of breathing ask what load the patient is carrying and whether it looks sustainable. The oxygen requirement asks how much support it takes to achieve the oxygenation we see. Mental state and the trajectory over time ask whether the patient is improving, deteriorating, or losing the ability to keep breathing. Correcting the answer to one question can leave the dangerous one untouched: oxygen can fix Patient B's saturation while his PaCO2 rises, and a steady saturation in Patient A can be bought with effort she cannot sustain.

principles.title: Pulse oximetry: saturation is not tension, and tension is not content
body: An oximeter estimates the fraction of hemoglobin that carries oxygen in arterial blood. It does not measure PaO2, and it does not measure oxygen content, which also depends on the hemoglobin concentration. The relation between saturation and tension is the sigmoid oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve. On its flat upper part, large changes in PaO2 produce small changes in saturation: a patient whose PaO2 falls from 150 to 90 mm Hg loses almost no saturation, so the oximeter cannot show the loss of that reserve. On the steep part, below roughly 60 mm Hg, small falls in tension produce large falls in saturation, which is why patients near 88 to 90 percent can desaturate rapidly.

The curve also moves. Acidemia, a raised PaCO2, fever, and higher concentrations of 2,3-diphosphoglycerate shift it to the right, so the same PaO2 gives a lower saturation. Alkalemia and hypothermia shift it to the left. This matters for Patients B and C. A PaO2 of about 56 mm Hg corresponds to about 88 percent on a standard curve at pH 7.40. Correcting a standard curve model for pH and carbon dioxide predicts roughly 80 percent for B, at pH 7.21 and PaCO2 70 mm Hg, and the mid 80s for C, at pH 7.31 and PaCO2 62 mm Hg. These are estimates from an average curve, not unique values: temperature, 2,3-diphosphoglycerate, and the individual's hemoglobin also shift it, and pH alone does not fix a saturation.

Oximeters have measurement error, and it is not evenly distributed. A widely cited 2020 analysis of paired oximeter and arterial measurements reported that occult hypoxemia, defined as an arterial saturation (SaO2) below 88 percent despite an SpO2 of 92 to 96 percent, was detected more often in Black patients than in White patients. Its size varies between devices and remains under study. The practical lesson does not depend on the exact figure: an oximeter reading at the lower end of a target range may conceal a lower true saturation, and an arterial sample is the check when decisions depend on it. Note that the saturation printed on many blood-gas reports is calculated from PaO2 and pH using a standard curve; only co-oximetry measures the hemoglobin species directly. Poor perfusion, motion, nail polish, and carboxyhemoglobin and methemoglobin can also mislead.
Finally, oxygen masks hypoventilation. Once Patient B is breathing supplemental oxygen, his saturation can be normal while his PaCO2 rises. An oximeter cannot see carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: A man pulled from a house fire is drowsy, with an SpO2 of 99 percent on a standard oximeter. Why might the oximeter be misleading, and what would show his true oxygen status?
questions.answer: Standard two-wavelength oximeters cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so in carbon monoxide poisoning they can report a near-normal saturation while much of the hemoglobin carries no oxygen. His PaO2 may also be normal, because PaO2 reflects dissolved oxygen and not what hemoglobin carries. Oxygen content, the quantity the tissues depend on, may be badly reduced. Co-oximetry on a blood sample measures the hemoglobin species directly and gives the true oxygenated fraction.
questions.causalChain: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin in place of oxygen; standard oximeters read carboxyhemoglobin as if it were oxyhemoglobin; displayed SpO2 stays high; true oxyhemoglobin and oxygen content fall; PaO2 can remain normal.
questions.assumption: That the device is a standard pulse oximeter rather than one designed to detect dyshemoglobins.
questions.misconception: That a normal SpO2 and a normal PaO2 together prove adequate oxygen delivery.

principles.title: Blood gases and capnography
body: An arterial blood gas gives PaO2, PaCO2, and pH at one moment. A venous gas is less invasive and is often used to screen for hypercapnia and to follow pH. Venous carbon dioxide (PvCO2) normally runs a few mm Hg above arterial PaCO2, but the two are not interchangeable: the gap depends on how much carbon dioxide each tissue adds and how fast blood flows through it, so in shock or poor regional perfusion it can widen unpredictably. A normal venous value makes significant arterial hypercapnia less likely; a raised one needs an arterial sample when the decision depends on the exact level. A venous gas tells us nothing reliable about arterial oxygen.

The pH places the carbon dioxide in time. When PaCO2 rises acutely, bicarbonate rises only a little, and pH falls considerably. When it has been high for days, the kidneys retain bicarbonate and pH returns toward normal. Patient C, with a PaCO2 of 62 mm Hg, a bicarbonate of 30 mmol/L, and a pH of 7.31, has an acute rise on top of chronic retention. Patient B, with a PaCO2 of 70 mm Hg, a bicarbonate of 27 mmol/L, and a pH near 7.21, has an acute problem. The same PaCO2 in each would carry different meanings.

Capnography measures carbon dioxide at the airway, continuously and breath by breath. Its waveform shows that a patient is breathing, its rate, and, in airway obstruction, a characteristic sloping shape. End-tidal carbon dioxide approximates arterial PaCO2 only when dead space is small. As alveolar dead space rises, end-tidal values fall below arterial ones by a widening and variable margin. A falling end-tidal value can therefore mean better ventilation, worse dead space, or a falling cardiac output, and the trend needs to be anchored to an arterial value.

principles.title: Indices of oxygenation and the ROX index
body: Several indices compress oxygenation and effort into one number. The PaO2/FiO2 ratio and its non-invasive counterpart, the SpO2/FiO2 ratio, describe how much oxygen is getting through for the oxygen given. Both depend on the level of support and on FiO2, as noted in Part III, and the SpO2-based version loses meaning once saturation reaches the flat top of the curve.

The ROX index, described in patients with pneumonia treated with high-flow nasal oxygen, combines oxygenation and breathing pattern: it is the SpO2/FiO2 ratio divided by the respiratory rate. It is best understood as a way of following a patient on high-flow oxygen over time. A falling index means that oxygenation is worsening relative to the oxygen given, that breathing is becoming faster, or both. Consider a patient whose SpO2 stays at 93 percent on an FiO2 of 0.6 while her rate rises from 26 to 36/min: her ROX falls from about 6.0 to about 4.3 with no change on the oximeter (illustrative numbers). In the original cohort, a ROX of 4.88 or more at 2, 6, or 12 hours was associated with avoiding intubation, and the index predicted better as time on high-flow oxygen passed. That anchor belongs to one population and to those time points. The index is a trend to watch, and it cannot override worsening consciousness, effort, or perfusion.

questions.prompt: Patient A is on high-flow nasal oxygen. Over two hours her SpO2 stays at 93 percent on the same FiO2, but her respiratory rate rises from 26 to 36/min and she is using accessory muscles. What does that tell you?
questions.answer: That she is maintaining oxygenation at the cost of increasing work. A stable saturation reflects only one side of the balance. Her rising rate and accessory muscle use show that the load on her pump is growing relative to its capacity, or that drive is rising, and her ROX index will have fallen even though SpO2 has not. Her PaCO2 may still be low or normal. This trajectory, not any single number, is what should prompt reassessment of whether high-flow oxygen is enough, including a review of the decision to intubate, which is discussed in Part VI.
questions.causalChain: Worsening pneumonia or rising demand increases load; drive increases; respiratory rate and muscle recruitment rise; saturation is defended by effort; capacity may not sustain the effort; the index combining rate and oxygenation falls before saturation does.
questions.assumption: That her FiO2 and flow were constant and that the rate rise is not mainly from pain, fever, or anxiety that can be treated separately.
questions.misconception: That a stable saturation means a stable patient.

principles.title: Part VI. Support matched to the mechanism
body: Support is chosen by asking which part has failed and what each intervention changes. Oxygen raises alveolar oxygen. High-flow systems add a steadier FiO2, washout of dead space, and a little pressure. Non-invasive ventilation adds pressure that can unload muscles and recruit lung. Intubation and mechanical ventilation take over the pump and protect the airway. None of them treats the underlying disease. This part describes the principles; settings, devices, and drugs belong elsewhere.

principles.title: Oxygen: devices, targets, and oxygen-induced hypercapnia
body: Oxygen devices fall into two families. Variable-performance devices, such as nasal cannulas, simple face masks, and masks with reservoir bags, deliver oxygen at a flow that is often lower than the patient's peak inspiratory flow. The patient draws in room air to make up the difference, so the FiO2 actually reaching the alveoli depends on how hard and fast the patient is breathing. A distressed patient breathing fast gets a lower FiO2 from the same device than a calm one. Fixed-performance devices, such as Venturi masks, entrain air at a set ratio and deliver a flow high enough to meet most inspiratory demand, so FiO2 is more predictable.

Oxygen is a drug with a target. Guidelines recommend titrating to a saturation range rather than giving as much as possible. The British Thoracic Society guideline sets a target of 94 to 98 percent for most acutely ill adults and 88 to 92 percent, or a patient-specific range, for those at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, such as people with COPD, obesity hypoventilation, or neuromuscular disease. The lower range is not a reason to withhold oxygen from a critically hypoxemic patient. The same guideline gives critically ill patients with these risk factors the usual initial target until a blood gas is available, and only then narrows the range or moves to supported ventilation. Initial resuscitation and ongoing titration are separate steps. A randomized prehospital trial in patients with suspected COPD exacerbation reported lower mortality with titrated oxygen than with high-flow oxygen, which is part of the evidence behind the lower target.

Why can oxygen raise PaCO2 in a patient like C? Several mechanisms contribute, and their relative weight is debated. First, high inspired oxygen releases hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction in poorly ventilated units, sending more blood to regions that clear carbon dioxide poorly and increasing effective dead space. Second, the Haldane effect: oxygenated hemoglobin carries less carbon dioxide, so as saturation rises, carbon dioxide is released into the plasma. Third, in some patients the drive to breathe falls a little when hypoxemia is relieved. The older teaching that the third mechanism dominates, that such patients breathe only because they are hypoxic, is now thought to overstate it. The consequence is the same whichever dominates: aiming for a normal saturation in Patient C can make his acidosis worse.

For Patient B the logic is different. Oxygen will correct his saturation easily and safely in the short term, but it treats a consequence. The cause, depressed drive from an opioid, needs its own treatment, and his ventilation must be watched through carbon dioxide and clinical signs rather than the oximeter.

principles.title: High-flow nasal oxygen
body: High-flow nasal oxygen delivers warmed, humidified gas at flows that can match or exceed a distressed patient's inspiratory flow. Several effects follow. Less room air is entrained, so the delivered FiO2 is closer to the set FiO2. The high flow washes carbon dioxide out of the nasopharynx at the end of each breath, reducing effective dead space and so the minute ventilation needed for a given PaCO2. A small positive pressure is generated in the airway, though its size depends on flow and on whether the mouth is open, and it is modest and variable. Warmth and humidity make the therapy tolerable for long periods, and many patients find it more comfortable than a mask.

For hypoxemic respiratory failure, the FLORALI trial compared high-flow oxygen with standard oxygen and with non-invasive ventilation in patients without hypercapnia. It found no significant difference in its primary outcome, the rate of intubation. Mortality at 90 days, a secondary outcome, was lower with high-flow oxygen, a finding that generates a hypothesis rather than settling the question. The 2022 European Respiratory Society guideline suggests high-flow oxygen over conventional oxygen, and over non-invasive ventilation, in hypoxemic respiratory failure. Both are conditional recommendations, meaning that the balance favors high-flow oxygen for most patients but the evidence leaves room for judgment.

For Patient A, high-flow oxygen can deliver a reliable FiO2 and reduce work through dead-space washout. It cannot open her consolidated lung to any great degree. Its success depends on whether her pneumonia improves before her effort becomes unsustainable, which is why the trajectory of her rate, effort, and oxygenation over hours matters more than the first reading.

questions.prompt: Patient A is moved from a reservoir face mask to high-flow nasal oxygen at a similar nominal oxygen concentration. Her respiratory rate is 32/min. Predict what changes and what does not.
questions.answer: Her delivered FiO2 is likely to rise toward the set value, because the high flow meets more of her inspiratory demand and less room air is entrained. Washout of nasopharyngeal dead space should lower the minute ventilation she needs for the same PaCO2, and the warmed, humidified gas is easier to tolerate, so her rate and effort may settle somewhat. What should not change much is her shunt: blood crossing consolidated lung still meets no inspired gas, so any rise in PaO2 is likely to be modest. Her course over the next hours, not the first reading, will show whether this is enough.
questions.causalChain: High flow meets inspiratory demand; entrainment falls and delivered FiO2 rises; dead-space washout lowers required ventilation; work may fall; unventilated units remain unventilated; PaO2 rises little if shunt dominates.
questions.assumption: That the flow set is high enough for her demand and that her mouth is mostly closed, which affects both washout and any pressure generated.
questions.misconception: That high-flow oxygen treats shunt the way it treats low V/Q or dead space.

principles.title: Non-invasive ventilation
body: Non-invasive ventilation applies positive pressure through a mask. Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) holds one pressure throughout the breath. Bilevel ventilation adds a higher inspiratory pressure to a lower expiratory one, and the two pressures do different things. The assistance to each breath comes mainly from the difference between them, the inspiratory pressure above the expiratory level. That difference takes over part of the work, increases tidal volume and alveolar ventilation, and so lowers PaCO2. The expiratory pressure has other jobs. In some hypoxemic patients it can recruit collapsed alveoli and improve oxygenation, an effect separate from unloading and carbon dioxide clearance. In a patient with intrinsic PEEP and expiratory flow limitation, a modest expiratory pressure set below the trapped pressure can reduce the effort needed to start each breath, because the muscles no longer have to overcome the whole threshold themselves. It is not a simple subtraction from intrinsic PEEP. Without flow limitation, or when set too high, external pressure can add to hyperinflation. Detailed titration is outside this chapter.

Patient C is the patient for whom the evidence is strongest. In COPD exacerbations with hypercapnic acidosis, non-invasive ventilation unloads tiring muscles, offsets intrinsic PEEP, and raises alveolar ventilation. The ERS/ATS guideline strongly recommends bilevel non-invasive ventilation when a COPD exacerbation causes respiratory acidosis with a pH of 7.35 or less, and recommends a trial of it even in a patient thought to need intubation, unless he is deteriorating immediately. The same guideline strongly recommends either bilevel non-invasive ventilation or CPAP for respiratory failure due to cardiogenic pulmonary edema (moderate certainty; patients in cardiogenic shock were excluded), a condition covered in the later [chapter on acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema](/cases/cardiogenic-pulmonary-edema#principle-cpap-niv). In de novo hypoxemic respiratory failure, the evidence is weaker and the role uncertain. One single-center trial in patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome reported fewer intubations with a helmet than with a face mask, but it was small and stopped early for efficacy, and its findings need confirmation.

Non-invasive ventilation needs a cooperative patient who can protect the airway, and it can fail silently in the hypoxemic patient, who may generate large tidal volumes and high transpulmonary pressures through the mask. It also has its own circulatory consequences, as positive pressure raises intrathoracic pressure. Applying it is a trial with a question: is the expected improvement happening?

questions.prompt: Suppose Patient C had instead been given oxygen at high flow by a reservoir mask before his first blood gas. An hour later his SpO2 is 97 percent, but he is drowsier and his PaCO2 has risen from 62 to 78 mm Hg. Which mechanisms could contribute?
questions.answer: Several, probably together. High inspired oxygen may have released hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, redirecting blood to poorly ventilated units and raising effective dead space. The Haldane effect releases carbon dioxide from hemoglobin as it becomes saturated. His drive may have fallen modestly once hypoxemia was relieved. Underneath all three, his pump was already overloaded, so it could not increase ventilation to compensate. His drowsiness is consistent with acute hypercapnia. The response is to lower oxygen to his target range and to support ventilation, for which non-invasive ventilation is the best-supported option in this setting, while avoiding abrupt removal of oxygen, which would let alveolar oxygen fall sharply while his PaCO2 is still high.
questions.causalChain: High FiO2 raises PAO2 in low V/Q units; vasoconstriction there is released; perfusion shifts toward poorly ventilated units; effective dead space rises; the Haldane effect adds carbon dioxide; drive may fall; an overloaded pump cannot raise ventilation; PaCO2 rises.
questions.assumption: That the two PaCO2 values are comparable arterial samples and that nothing else, such as a sedative, was given.
questions.misconception: That oxygen-induced hypercapnia is only loss of hypoxic drive. More of the effect is usually attributed to worsened matching and the Haldane effect.

principles.title: Deciding to intubate, and where this chapter stops
body: The decision to intubate is a judgment about trajectory, not a threshold on one number. The questions are whether the patient can protect the airway, whether mental state is falling, whether effort is sustainable, whether the expected improvement on high-flow oxygen or non-invasive ventilation has happened in the window that was set when it began, and whether there is concurrent shock that the work of breathing is making worse. An improving patient with poor numbers may be on the right path, and a patient with acceptable numbers bought by escalating effort may not be.

Some observational studies have associated later intubation, after failure of high-flow oxygen or non-invasive ventilation, with worse outcomes. One retrospective single-center study of 175 patients in whom high-flow oxygen failed reported ICU mortality of 39.2 percent when intubation came within 48 hours and 66.7 percent when it came later. These are associations. Sicker patients both fail non-invasive support and do worse, and the studies cannot fully separate the effect of delay from the effect of severity. The finding supports a clear plan for what would count as failure, set in advance, rather than a rule for intubating earlier.

The physiology of intubating a patient in respiratory failure, including desaturation during apnea and the collapse of the circulation after induction and positive pressure, is the subject of the [chapter on the physiologically difficult airway](/cases/physiologically-difficult-airway).

Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a boundary for this chapter. It describes acute, diffuse, inflammatory lung injury with permeability edema, shunt, and stiff lungs, from causes such as pneumonia, sepsis, aspiration, or trauma. Patient A may meet its criteria if her disease spreads. A 2024 global definition broadened the criteria, including patients treated with high-flow oxygen and oxygenation assessed by oximetry, and European and American guidelines from 2023 and 2024 address its respiratory support. Its management, including lung-protective ventilation, prone positioning, and the use of PEEP, deserves a chapter of its own and is not covered here.

principles.title: Part VII. Reassessment and synthesis
body: Every intervention in respiratory failure comes with a prediction. If the mechanism has been identified correctly, specific things should change, in a specific direction, over a specific time. Reassessment asks whether they have.

principles.title: What should improve, and when
body: After oxygen, saturation should rise within minutes. A brisk rise argues against a large shunt contribution; a small rise supports one, though a low delivered FiO2 or a falling mixed venous content can blunt the response too. The response helps assess the likely contribution of shunt, but does not measure it in isolation. Either way, the oximeter's response says nothing about carbon dioxide.

After high-flow oxygen or non-invasive ventilation, the respiratory rate and visible effort should begin to settle, and saturation should hold on the same or lower FiO2. In a hypercapnic patient on non-invasive ventilation, pH, PaCO2, respiratory rate, and work of breathing should start to improve within about the first hour or two; the ERS/ATS guideline lists failure to improve after an hour among the early predictors that the trial will fail. Some signs do not wait for a scheduled check. Worsening consciousness, rising effort, inability to tolerate the mask, or hemodynamic instability mean the trial is failing now, and intubation should be considered now. A flat trajectory with stable mental state allows a short search for a correctable cause, such as a mask leak or poor synchrony, but not an open-ended wait.

After reversal of a drug or treatment of a mechanical cause, such as relief of a pneumothorax, the improvement should be prompt. If it is not, the diagnosis needs revisiting. The thread through all of these is the same as in shock: escalate on trajectory rather than on a single value, and be ready to change your view of the mechanism when the response does not fit.

questions.prompt: Patient C has been on non-invasive ventilation for an hour, with oxygen titrated to his target range. His PaCO2 has gone from 62 to 61 mm Hg, his pH is unchanged at 7.31, and he is drowsier than on arrival. What would make you reconsider the mechanism or the plan?
questions.answer: The lack of meaningful change in PaCO2 and pH after an hour, together with a worsening mental state, argues that ventilation is not being effectively supported. Failure to improve after an hour is itself an early predictor of NIV failure, and the drowsiness makes this urgent rather than something to recheck later. Look quickly for practical failures: a large mask leak, poor synchrony between the ventilator and his breathing, too little inspiratory pressure above the expiratory level, or an expiratory pressure poorly matched to his trapped pressure. At the same time, reconsider the diagnosis: a pneumothorax, a large secretion load, a pneumonia or pulmonary embolism adding shunt or dead space, or drowsiness from a cause other than carbon dioxide, such as a sedative. If nothing is quickly correctable, or his consciousness falls further, invasive ventilation should be considered now.
questions.causalChain: Non-invasive ventilation should raise alveolar ventilation and offset intrinsic PEEP; PaCO2 should fall and pH rise; an absent response means support is not reaching the alveoli, the load has grown, or the diagnosis is incomplete.
questions.assumption: That the blood gases are arterial and comparable and that the settings and interface were assessed before judging failure.
questions.misconception: That a small fall in PaCO2 means the treatment is working. A response that does not change pH or mental state is not yet a response.

questions.prompt: Patient B's opioid effect is reversed and his respiratory rate and depth return toward normal. On room air, predict what happens to his PaCO2, PAO2, A–a gradient, and SpO2, and what could still go wrong.
questions.answer: As alveolar ventilation rises, PaCO2 should fall toward normal over minutes, not instantly, because carbon dioxide stores must empty. From the alveolar gas equation, PAO2 rises as PaCO2 falls; at a PaCO2 of 40 mm Hg it would be about 100 mm Hg. His A–a gradient should stay normal, and his PaO2 and SpO2 should rise with PAO2. What could still go wrong is recurrence: if the reversing effect wears off before the opioid has cleared, ventilation can fall again, and a patient who has been put on oxygen meanwhile may show no warning on the oximeter. Aspiration during the period of reduced consciousness could also add a lung problem that would widen his gradient.
questions.causalChain: Reversal restores drive; alveolar ventilation rises; PaCO2 falls; PAO2 = 150 − PaCO2/0.8 rises; with normal lungs, PaO2 and SpO2 follow PAO2 and the gradient stays normal.
questions.assumption: That his lungs remain normal, without aspiration, and that he stays on room air so the oximeter still reflects ventilation.
questions.misconception: That one good response means the problem is over.

principles.title: Back to the three patients
body: Patient A had a widened A–a gradient and a weak response to oxygen: shunt through consolidated lung. Oxygen alone was never going to correct her, and her danger was rising effort. She needed a reliable FiO2, support for her work of breathing, treatment of the pneumonia, and close watch on her trajectory, with a decision about intubation made on that trajectory rather than on her saturation.

Patient B had a normal A–a gradient and a high PaCO2: hypoventilation from depressed drive, in normal lungs. His saturation, roughly 80 percent on room air, corrected easily with oxygen, and that was the risk, because it could have hidden a rising PaCO2. He needed treatment of the drug effect, airway protection, and monitoring of ventilation, through carbon dioxide and clinical signs, rather than through the oximeter.

Patient C had high airway resistance, air trapping, intrinsic PEEP, and an overloaded pump. On arrival his PaCO2 was 62 mm Hg with a PaO2 of 56 mm Hg on room air, so his PAO2 was about 150 − 62/0.8 ≈ 72 mm Hg and his A–a gradient about 16 mm Hg, with a saturation in the mid 80s. That gradient is inside the rough range expected at his age, so his gas is explained almost entirely by hypoventilation on a background of chronic retention. His COPD makes mismatched lung units very likely, but the gas alone does not prove them. Too much oxygen could have made him worse. He needed oxygen titrated to 88 to 92 percent, non-invasive ventilation to unload his muscles and offset his trapped pressure, treatment of the exacerbation, and reassessment within the first hour or two, sooner if his consciousness or effort worsened.

questions.prompt: A man with severe obesity arrives drowsy with a high PaCO2, an acidemic pH, and an SpO2 in the mid 80s on room air. His chest is clear. Which of the three patients does his physiology resemble, and what does that imply for oxygen and support?
questions.answer: He resembles Patient B in that hypoventilation explains much of his hypoxemia, and Patient C in that the problem is a pump facing a heavy load, here from the chest wall and abdomen rather than from the airways. The A–a gradient may be normal or only modestly widened, depending on how much basal atelectasis he has. Like C, he is at risk of oxygen-induced hypercapnia, so oxygen should be titrated to 88 to 92 percent while urgent blood gases are pending, then adjusted using the gases and his response. Correcting his saturation alone would leave the ventilatory failure untreated; support that raises alveolar ventilation addresses the mechanism, and his pH, mental state, and PaCO2 are the measures of whether it is working.
questions.causalChain: Heavy chest wall and abdominal load reduce compliance and tidal volume; alveolar ventilation falls; PaCO2 rises and PAO2 falls; dependent atelectasis may add shunt; high oxygen can worsen matching and hypercapnia; assisted ventilation raises alveolar ventilation.
questions.assumption: That no other cause of reduced drive, such as a sedative, and no acute lung disease is present.
questions.misconception: That a clear chest and a correctable saturation mean the problem is minor.

principles.title: Synthesis
body: The same saturation hid three failures. Carbon dioxide, never seen by the oximeter, reports on ventilation, and the alveolar gas equation shows how much of the hypoxemia that ventilation explains. A clearly widened A–a gradient points to the lung; a normal one points away from a transfer defect without proving healthy lungs. The response to oxygen helps assess the likely contribution of shunt, but does not measure it in isolation, because delivered FiO2 and mixed venous oxygen content also change the result. The pattern and effort of breathing show load and capacity. Support works best when it is chosen for the part that has failed, and it is judged by whether the predicted changes happen, on a timescale set in advance and cut short when mental state or effort worsens.

treatmentApproach.title: Recognize which part is failing
treatmentApproach.action: Assess SpO2, respiratory rate and pattern, effort, mental status, and a blood gas, and ask whether the problem is oxygenation, ventilation, the pump, or a combination.
treatmentApproach.why: The same saturation can hide shunt, hypoventilation, or an overloaded pump, and each needs different support.

treatmentApproach.title: Treat what can be reversed now
treatmentApproach.action: Look for and treat immediately reversible causes, such as opioid toxicity, airway obstruction, tension pneumothorax, and bronchospasm.
treatmentApproach.why: Some failures have a single cause whose removal restores function faster than any form of support.

treatmentApproach.title: Give oxygen to a target range
treatmentApproach.action: Titrate oxygen to the appropriate range: generally 94 to 98 percent, or 88 to 92 percent for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure pending urgent blood gases. In critical illness, provide immediate oxygen and resuscitation, then adjust oxygen and ventilatory support promptly using blood gases and the clinical response. Never withhold oxygen from a critically hypoxemic patient, and remember it does not treat hypoventilation.
treatmentApproach.why: Oxygen corrects hypoxemia from most causes but can mask rising carbon dioxide and can worsen hypercapnia in at-risk patients.

treatmentApproach.title: Match support to the mechanism
treatmentApproach.action: Choose high-flow oxygen, non-invasive ventilation, or intubation according to the failing part, and state in advance what response is expected and by when.
treatmentApproach.why: Each form of support changes specific things; a stated expectation turns support into a testable trial.

treatmentApproach.title: Reassess on trajectory
treatmentApproach.action: Recheck effort, rate, mental status, oxygenation for the FiO2 given, and carbon dioxide and pH within about the first hour of non-invasive support. Escalate on the trend, and at once if consciousness or effort is worsening.
treatmentApproach.why: Saturation can be stable while load outpaces capacity, and PaCO2 can rise late.
